sq.ANSWER:
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

 

struct Node {

    int roll;

    Node* next;

};

 

// Function to delete a node by value (roll number)

void deleteNode(Node*& head, int key) {

    if (head == nullptr) return; // Empty list

 

    Node *curr = head, *prev = nullptr;

 

    // Case 1: Single node in the list

    if (head->roll == key && head->next == head) {

        delete head;

        head = nullptr;

        return;

    }

 

    // Case 2: Deleting head node

    if (head->roll == key) {

        // Find last node to update its next pointer

        Node* last = head;

        while (last->next != head)

            last = last->next;

 

        last->next = head->next;

        Node* temp = head;

        head = head->next;

        delete temp;

        return;

    }

 

    // Case 3: Deleting middle or end node

    prev = head;

    curr = head->next;

    while (curr != head && curr->roll != key) {

        prev = curr;

        curr = curr->next;

    }

 

    if (curr == head) {

        cout << "Roll number " << key << " not found.\n";

        return;

    }

 

    prev->next = curr->next;

    delete curr;

}

• A doubly linked list or a two-way linked list is a more complex type of linked list which contains a pointer to the next as well as the previous node in the sequence. Therefore, it consists of three parts—data, a pointer to the next node, and a pointer to the previous node.

Figure: Doubly linked list

In C, the structure of a doubly linked list can be given as,

The PREV field of the first node and the NEXT field of the last node will contain NULL. The PREV field is used to store the address of the preceding node, which enables us to traverse the list in the backward direction.

Figure: Memory representation of a doubly linked list

  • In this example, START = 1, so the first data is stored at address 1, which is H. Since this is the first node, it has no previous node and hence stores NULL or –1 in the PREV field.
  • We will traverse the list until we reach a position where the NEXT entry contains –1 or NULL. This denotes the end of the linked list.
  • When we traverse the DATA and NEXT in this manner, we will finally see that the linked list in the above example stores characters that when put together form the word HELLO.

Inserting a New Node in a Doubly Linked List

  • Case 1: The new node is inserted at the beginning.
  • Case 2: The new node is inserted at the end.
  • Case 3: The new node is inserted after a given node.
  • Case 4: The new node is inserted before a given node.

 

Advantages of DLL over Singly Linked List:

  1. Bidirectional Traversal:
    You can move in both directions, unlike singly linked lists which only go forward.
  2. Easier Deletion:
    A node can be deleted without traversing from the head if you have a pointer to it.
  3. Reversible:
    The list can be easily reversed using pointers without extra space.

#include <stdio.h>

#include <stdlib.h>

// Node structure representing a player

struct Player {

    int id;

    struct Player* next;

};

// Function to insert at end (used for setup)

void insertAtEnd(struct Player** head, int id) {

    struct Player* newNode = (struct Player*)malloc(sizeof(struct Player));

    newNode->id = id;

    if (*head == NULL) {

        newNode->next = newNode;

        *head = newNode;

        return;

    }

    struct Player* temp = *head;

    while (temp->next != *head) {

        temp = temp->next;

    }

    temp->next = newNode;

    newNode->next = *head;

}

 

// Function to delete from beginning

void deleteFromBeginning(struct Player** head) {

    if (*head == NULL) {

        printf("Lobby is empty.\n");

        return;

    }

    struct Player* temp = *head;

    // Only one player

    if ((*head)->next == *head) {

        printf("Deleted player: %d (host)\n", temp->id);

        free(temp);

        *head = NULL;

        return;

    }

    struct Player* last = *head;

    while (last->next != *head)

        last = last->next;

    printf("Deleted player: %d (host)\n", (*head)->id);

    last->next = (*head)->next;

    *head = (*head)->next;

    free(temp);

}

// Function to delete from end

void deleteFromEnd(struct Player** head) {

    if (*head == NULL) {

        printf("Lobby is empty.\n");

        return;

    }

    struct Player* temp = *head;

    // Only one player

    if (temp->next == *head) {

        printf("Deleted player: %d (last remaining)\n", temp->id);

        free(temp);

        *head = NULL;

        return;

    }

    struct Player* prev = NULL;

    while (temp->next != *head) {

        prev = temp;

        temp = temp->next;

    }

 

    printf("Deleted player: %d (last player)\n", temp->id);

    prev->next = *head;

    free(temp);

}

// Function to display the lobby

void displayLobby(struct Player* head) {

    if (head == NULL) {

        printf("Lobby is empty.\n");

        return;

    }

    struct Player* temp = head;

    printf("Players in lobby: ");

    do {

        printf("%d -> ", temp->id);

        temp = temp->next;

    } while (temp != head);

    printf("(back to host)\n");

}

// Main function

int main() {

    struct Player* lobby = NULL;

    // Add some players

    insertAtEnd(&lobby, 1); // Host

    insertAtEnd(&lobby, 2);

    insertAtEnd(&lobby, 3);

    insertAtEnd(&lobby, 4);

 

    displayLobby(lobby);

    // Host leaves

    deleteFromBeginning(&lobby);

    displayLobby(lobby);

    // Last player leaves

    deleteFromEnd(&lobby);

    displayLobby(lobby);

    return 0;

}
